programme: Infinite populations · structure and port schedules

plain_language.question: What structure follows from the critical parent/child balance, and when does it realize every infinite word?
plain_language.what_we_learned: Persistent minimum crossing width fixes the tail adjacency. Every critical population has an exact legal fair finite-port encoding; full-schedule periodicity separately forces universality.
plain_language.what_it_lets_someone_do: Replace the infinite tail with an exact port representation and apply the periodic realization theorem only when its genuine labelled-schedule hypothesis is established.
plain_language.what_cannot_conclude: The encoder does not make arbitrary schedules periodic or every critical population universal; rigidity is not a word-language theorem.

exact_statement_and_scope: Three distinct statements concern the existing naturally indexed simple InfiniteLabeledPopulation k k, with finite root support, a parent of every required label at each nonroot and child cap k. (1) Rigidity: if every sufficiently late actual cut has crossing count k(k+1)/2, the eventual adjacency is exactly u→v iff u<v≤u+k. One attaining cut does not give this tail conclusion, and adjacency alone does not establish arbitrary-label universality. (2) Encoding, without minimum-width or periodicity assumptions: eventual_encoding constructs a root-free base, C equal to the actual crossing count, initial tokens and a legal fair C-slot schedule; decoded labelled edges agree exactly for every target beyond the base, including edges from pre-base sources, and every actual tail label is below k. Classical finite bijections are used; no regularity, enumeration or fairness is an extra population premise. (3) Conditional realization: if the constructed full named-slot/replacement-label schedule is eventually periodic with positive period p, every infinite word has a strict actual path beginning within one period of that tail. Finite slots do not imply periodicity. The pre-base graph is not reconstructed by the decoder.
